_note: AI-drafted Igbo A1 grammar lessons for Langi, not yet reviewed by a native speaker. Slugs match the ig catalog in lib/grammar.ts. Drill cues give the meaning, never the answer. Seeded by `npx tsx scripts/seed-grammar-ng.ts ig`. In examples, `fr` holds the Igbo sentence (field name kept from the original schema).

lessons.summary: m, ị, ọ, anyị, unu and ha mean I, you, he/she/it, we, you (plural) and they.
lessons.explanation:
Igbo has no he or she: ọ covers he, she and it. The subject pronouns are m (I), ị (you), ọ (he, she, it), anyị (we), unu (you, plural) and ha (they).

For I, the m often comes after the verb word: Ana m eri nri (I am eating food). With the others the pronoun comes first: Ị na-eri nri (You are eating food), Ọ na-ere ahịa (He/she is selling goods), Anyị na-agụ akwụkwọ (We are reading).

The dots under ị, ọ and ụ matter. They are separate letters, so keep them.

drills.prompt: Ana ___ eri nri. (I am eating food)

lessons.summary: na- shows an action in progress, aga- shows the future, and a verb ending in -ra or -rọ shows the past.
lessons.explanation:
Igbo shows time with a small word or an ending on the verb.

Progressive: na- plus the verb, Ọ na-eri nri (He/she is eating). With m (I) you say Ana m: Ana m eri nri.

Future: aga plus the verb, Aga m eri nri (I will eat food), Aga m abịa (I will come).

Past: many verbs add an ending such as -ra or -rọ: Ọ bịara ụnyaahụ (He/she came yesterday), Ọ gara ahịa (He/she went to the market).

drills.prompt: Ọ ___ ahịa. (He/she went to the market)
___ m eri nri. (I will eat food)
Ana m ___ nri. (I am eating food)
Ọ na-___ nri. (He/she is eating food)

lessons.summary: Use bụ for what someone is, nọ for where someone is. Describing words work like verbs.
lessons.explanation:
Igbo splits to be into two verbs.

bụ links a person to an identity: Abụ m onye nkụzi (I am a teacher), Ọ bụ nne m (She is my mother).

nọ says where someone is: Anọ m n'ụlọ (I am at home), Ha nọ n'ahịa (They are at the market).

Describing words are verbs in Igbo, so you do not need to add to be: Nwa ahụ mara mma (The child is beautiful).

drills.prompt: ___ m onye nkụzi. (I am a teacher)
Ha ___ n'ahịa. (They are at the market)
Ọ ___ nne m. (She is my mother)
Nwa ahụ ___ mma. (The child is beautiful)

lessons.summary: Add -ghị to the verb to say not: Anaghị m eri anụ (I do not eat meat).
lessons.explanation:
Igbo makes a negative with the ending -ghị on the verb.

Present: Anaghị m eri anụ (I do not eat meat), Ọ naghị abịa (He/she does not come). Future: Anyị agaghị aga (We will not go). Past: Erighị m nri (I did not eat), Aghọtaghị m (I do not understand).

Notice the m follows the negative verb, just as it does in the positive.

drills.prompt: Anaghị ___ eri anụ. (I do not eat meat)
___ m nri. (I did not eat food)

lessons.summary: Gịnị (what), onye (who), ebee (where), kedu (how) and ole (how much) open a question.
lessons.explanation:
A yes/no question can be the same sentence with a rising voice, or it can end with a question tone.

For information questions, start with the question word: Gịnị bụ aha gị? (What is your name?), Onye bụ nna gị? (Who is your father?), Ebee ka ị na-ebi? (Where do you live?), Kedu ka ị mere? (How are you?), Ole ka ọ bụ? (How much is it?).

ka is often placed after the question word before the verb.

drills.prompt: ___ bụ aha gị? (What is your name?)
___ ka ị na-ebi? (Where do you live?)
___ ka ọ bụ? (How much is it?)
___ bụ nna gị? (Who is your father?)

lessons.summary: Put the owner after the noun: ụlọ m (my house), ụlọ nna m (my father's house).
lessons.explanation:
The owner comes after the thing, with no extra word: ụlọ m (house my, my house), ụlọ gị (your house), ụlọ ya (his/her house), ụlọ anyị (our house), ụlọ unu (your house, plural) and ụlọ ha (their house).

To say someone's house, put the owner's name after the noun: ụlọ nna m (my father's house).

lessons.summary: Igbo nouns stay the same. Use ndị or ụmụ before the noun, or a number after it.
lessons.explanation:
Most Igbo nouns do not change in the plural. Put ndị before a word for people: ndị nkụzi (teachers). Use ụmụ for children and young ones: ụmụ akwụkwọ (students, children of school).

A number after the noun makes it plural without any other change: mmadụ atọ (three people). ọtụtụ means many: ọtụtụ mmadụ (many people).

lessons.summary: Greet with Ndewo and Nnọọ, ask with Biko, thank with Daalụ, and give a command with the plain verb.
lessons.explanation:
A command in Igbo is the verb on its own: Bịa ebe a (Come here), Gaa n'ụlọ (Go home), Rie nri (Eat food), Nọdụ ala (Sit down).

Soften it with biko (please): Biko, nye m mmiri (Please, give me water). Thank someone with daalụ. Ndewo means hello and nnọọ means welcome.

drills.prompt: ___, nye m mmiri. (Please, give me water)
